subtopic_detail: discordance between pubic hair development and testicular volume in a tall adolescent boy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 15 year old boy referred by his school because of longstanding difficulty with reading and written work and because he finds it hard to make friends. His parents also wonder whether he is developing normally.

He is taller than both parents were at his age, and his height sits on the 97th centile against a mid parental centile of 40. His arm span exceeds his height by 7 cm. He has adult type pubic hair and has been shaving occasionally for a year. On examination his testes measure 4 mL on each side by orchidometer and he has firm breast tissue palpable behind both nipples. He takes no medication and uses no supplements.

data_table.Examination: Height on the 97th centile, arm span exceeding height by 7 cm, pubic hair Tanner stage 4, testicular volume 4 mL bilaterally and firm to palpation, bilateral glandular breast tissue, no abdominal or scrotal mass
data_table.Investigations: Luteinising hormone raised, follicle stimulating hormone raised, testosterone at the lower end of the reference range for age, prolactin within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat early morning testosterone with sex hormone binding globulin
options.rationale: Repeating the androgen measurement refines a number that is already consistent with the clinical picture, and the raised gonadotrophins have already localised the lesion to the testis. It delays the test that gives the answer. (Source: RCH CPG: Puberty)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa with contrast
options.rationale: Pituitary imaging is indicated when gonadotrophins are low or inappropriately normal alongside a low testosterone, which indicates a central cause. Here the gonadotrophins are raised, which places the defect in the testis and makes the pituitary the wrong organ to image. (Source: RCH CPG: Puberty)

options.text: Scrotal ultrasound to assess testicular volume and architecture
options.rationale: Ultrasound would confirm what the orchidometer has already established and is used principally to look for a testicular tumour, which would present with a discrete mass and typically with high oestrogen rather than raised gonadotrophins. It does not explain the tall stature or the learning profile. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.text: Peripheral blood karyotype requested through the clinical genetics service
options.rationale: Small firm testes that have failed to enlarge despite advanced pubic hair development, tall stature with long limbs, gynaecomastia and raised gonadotrophins with a low testosterone indicate primary testicular failure with a chromosomal basis, and a karyotype is the definitive test. Making the diagnosis opens access to androgen replacement, fertility preservation counselling and educational support. (Source: RCH CPG: Puberty)

options.text: Radiograph of the left hand and wrist to determine the bone age
options.rationale: Bone age is valuable when the question is the timing of puberty relative to growth, as in constitutional delay or precocity. His puberty has clearly begun and progressed, so the question is why the testes have not grown with it. (Source: RCH CPG: Puberty)

explanation.summary: Klinefelter syndrome, most often a 47,XXY karyotype, affects around one in 600 male births and is the commonest chromosomal cause of primary hypogonadism, yet the majority of affected men are never diagnosed. The reason is that puberty usually begins and progresses normally under adrenal and early testicular androgen drive, so pubic hair, voice change and body habitus develop on schedule, while progressive seminiferous tubule fibrosis prevents the testes from enlarging beyond about 4 to 6 mL. That discordance between advanced pubic hair and persistently small firm testes is the single most useful clinical clue and is easily missed if testicular volume is not measured. Additional features include tall stature with disproportionately long limbs from delayed epiphyseal closure, gynaecomastia, and a characteristic profile of language based learning difficulty with relatively preserved non verbal reasoning alongside social difficulties. Biochemically the picture is hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism, and management involves testosterone replacement from mid puberty, discussion of fertility preservation because sperm retrieval rates fall with age, and educational and psychological support.
key_points: Advanced pubic hair with testes still at 4 mL is the discriminating discordance
Raised gonadotrophins localise the defect to the testis rather than the pituitary
Tall stature with long limbs reflects delayed epiphyseal closure
The learning profile is typically language based with preserved non verbal reasoning
Discuss fertility preservation early because sperm retrieval rates decline with age
explanation.pearls: Measure testicular volume with an orchidometer in any tall adolescent boy referred for learning or social difficulties; a volume that remains at or below 6 mL once pubic hair has reached Tanner stage 4 should prompt a karyotype rather than reassurance.

subtopic_detail: ear position distinguishing a fused suture from positional moulding in occipital flattening
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 6 month old girl whose parents are worried about the shape of the back of her head. They first noticed flattening on the right at about three months of age. She sleeps on her back as they were advised, and they have tried turning her head to the other side at night without any change.

She is meeting her developmental milestones, feeds well and has no vomiting or irritability. Looking down on the top of her head from above, you see that the right ear sits further back and lower than the left, and that the left side of her forehead is more prominent than the right. There is a firm ridge palpable running across the back right of her skull and a bulge behind the right ear.

data_table.Examination: Right occipital flattening, right ear displaced posteriorly and inferiorly relative to the left, contralateral left frontal bossing, palpable ridge over the right lambdoid suture, ipsilateral mastoid bulge, anterior fontanelle soft, head circumference tracking the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Neurological examination normal, red reflex present and symmetrical, no papilloedema visualised, developmental milestones age appropriate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for neck stretches and tummy time coaching
options.rationale: Neck restriction commonly drives positional flattening and physiotherapy is central to managing that pathway, which is why this option is plausible. Her neck movement is not described as restricted and the ear displacement here is backwards rather than forwards, which is the opposite of the positional pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Give repositioning advice and review the head shape in two months
options.rationale: Repositioning is the correct treatment for deformation caused by external pressure, and it has already been tried without effect. A fused suture cannot remodel in response to positioning, so two further months would be lost. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

options.text: Refer for a moulding helmet to be fitted in the next four weeks
options.rationale: Helmet therapy is an option for moderate to severe positional deformity in selected infants within a defined age window. Applying a helmet to a skull with a fused suture does not correct the underlying restriction and delays the operation. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

options.text: Arrange plain skull radiographs and review the result in the clinic
options.rationale: Plain films are insensitive for sutural fusion in infancy and a normal film would not exclude the diagnosis, while an abnormal one would still be followed by specialist referral and dedicated imaging. The referral is what changes management. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.text: Refer to the craniofacial surgical service for specialist assessment
options.rationale: A palpable sutural ridge with the ear displaced backwards and downwards, a mastoid bulge and bossing of the opposite forehead describes a trapezoid head shape that indicates a fused suture rather than external moulding. Premature fusion requires surgical assessment and operative correction is generally undertaken within the first year. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

explanation.summary: Occipital flattening in infancy is usually positional and has become much more common since back sleeping was adopted for sudden infant death prevention, but a small proportion represents premature fusion of the lambdoid suture, and the two are separated at the bedside by looking down on the skull from above. Positional deformity produces a parallelogram: the flattened occiput pushes the ear on that side forwards and the forehead on the same side becomes more prominent. Lambdoid synostosis produces a trapezoid: the ear on the affected side is pulled backwards and downwards, there is a compensatory bulge over the mastoid, and the bossing appears on the opposite forehead. A palpable ridge along the suture supports fusion, and the absence of any response to sustained repositioning is further evidence against a positional cause. Positional deformity is managed with repositioning, tummy time and treatment of any associated neck restriction, with helmet therapy for selected moderate to severe cases, whereas fusion requires craniofacial referral and surgical correction, typically within the first year, to prevent progressive asymmetry and to protect brain growth.
key_points: Look down on the skull from above to judge parallelogram against trapezoid
Positional flattening pushes the ipsilateral ear forwards and bosses the ipsilateral forehead
Lambdoid fusion pulls the ipsilateral ear backwards and downwards with a mastoid bulge
Contralateral frontal bossing and a palpable sutural ridge indicate fusion
Failure to respond to sustained repositioning argues against a positional cause
explanation.pearls: The direction of ear displacement is the single most reliable bedside discriminator in occipital flattening: an ear pushed forward means positional moulding, an ear pulled backward and down means lambdoid synostosis and a craniofacial referral.

subtopic_detail: biphasic noisy breathing unchanged by position in an ex preterm infant with previous intubation
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4 month old girl in the emergency department with noisy breathing. She was born at 27 weeks gestation and was ventilated through an endotracheal tube for three weeks in the neonatal unit.

Her parents say the noise started at about three weeks after she came home and has slowly become louder. It is present when she breathes in and also when she breathes out, and they have not been able to find any position that makes it better or worse. This is her third presentation in two months with what has each time been treated as croup, and on each occasion she improved for a day and then returned to her usual noisy breathing. She is feeding adequately and growing along the 25th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148, blood pressure 82/48, respiratory rate 52, SpO2 95 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Biphasic stridor audible at rest and unchanged by prone or supine positioning, mild intercostal and subcostal recession, no drooling, chest otherwise clear, no cyanosis
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, no fever documented at any of the three presentations, growth tracking the 25th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to ear nose and throat for microlaryngoscopy and bronchoscopy
options.rationale: Stridor that is biphasic, unaltered by position and recurrent in an infant with prolonged neonatal intubation points to a fixed narrowing at or below the vocal cords rather than to a dynamic supraglottic collapse. Direct visualisation of the airway under anaesthesia is the only way to establish the site and severity and to plan treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

options.text: Commence a proton pump inhibitor trial and review in six weeks
options.rationale: Acid reflux aggravates supraglottic collapse and antireflux treatment is sometimes used as an adjunct in that condition. It does nothing for a fixed structural narrowing, and six weeks of observation in an infant with recession at rest carries a real risk of decompensation during the next viral illness. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

options.text: Reassure the parents that the noise resolves by eighteen months
options.rationale: Spontaneous resolution by around eighteen to twenty four months describes laryngomalacia, which is the commonest cause of infant stridor and the reason this reassurance is so tempting. That condition gives inspiratory stridor that worsens when supine, during feeding and when crying, and improves in the prone position, which is the opposite of what is described. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

options.text: Arrange a chest radiograph and review the film in the clinic
options.rationale: A chest film may show a vascular ring or a lower airway abnormality and is a reasonable adjunct, but it images below the level where the obstruction almost certainly lies and a normal film would not exclude it. It does not substitute for direct visualisation. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.text: Give nebulised adrenaline with oral dexamethasone and review after
options.rationale: This is the treatment for viral laryngotracheobronchitis and explains why she has transiently improved at each previous presentation, since reducing mucosal oedema temporarily widens an already narrowed lumen. Treating the recurring exacerbation again without investigating the fixed narrowing beneath it repeats the error of the previous two visits. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: The character and timing of stridor localise the obstruction: inspiratory stridor arises above the vocal cords, expiratory noise arises in the intrathoracic airway, and biphasic stridor indicates a fixed narrowing at the level of the glottis or subglottis where flow is limited in both phases of respiration. Laryngomalacia accounts for the majority of infant stridor and is distinguished by being inspiratory, worse supine and during feeding or crying, better prone, and by improving spontaneously over the first two years. Acquired subglottic stenosis follows prolonged or traumatic endotracheal intubation, which makes ex preterm infants the principal risk group, and it characteristically presents with biphasic stridor unaffected by position that becomes symptomatic during intercurrent viral illness. Recurrent croup, particularly more than twice in a year or in an infant under six months, is a recognised presentation of an underlying fixed narrowing and is an indication for airway assessment rather than for further episodic treatment. Microlaryngoscopy and bronchoscopy establish the grade of stenosis, which determines whether observation, endoscopic dilatation or open reconstruction is appropriate.
key_points: Biphasic stridor indicates a fixed glottic or subglottic narrowing
Laryngomalacia is inspiratory, worse supine and better prone, and resolves by about two years
Prolonged neonatal intubation is the main risk factor for acquired subglottic stenosis
Recurrent croup under six months of age warrants airway assessment
Microlaryngoscopy and bronchoscopy grade the stenosis and direct treatment
explanation.pearls: Two or more episodes of croup before six months of age, or any croup that does not fully settle between episodes, should prompt referral for airway endoscopy rather than another course of dexamethasone, because acquired subglottic stenosis presents exactly this way.
